statement: Four friends stand in a line. Going from left to right, each friend writes down one of the numbers $1$, $2$ or $3$, and no friend may write the same number as the friend directly to their left. How many different lists of four numbers are possible?

choices.misconception: I gave the first friend 3 choices and the next two friends 2 choices each, and forgot about the fourth friend, so I got 3 times 2 times 2.
I gave every friend 2 choices, including the first friend, who has no one to their left and really has 3 choices.
I counted four restrictions for four friends, giving 3 times 2 to the fourth power, but only three friends have someone to their left.
I ignored the rule and let every friend write any of the 3 numbers, so I got 3 to the fourth power.

hints: Count the choices friend by friend, from left to right.
The first friend is free. Each later friend only has to avoid one number, the one just written, so the count of choices does not depend on what came before.
The first friend has $3$ choices and each of the other three has $2$, so the total is $3 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2$.

solutions.reliable: The first friend may write any of $3$ numbers. The second friend must avoid the first friend's number, leaving $2$ choices, whatever that number was. The same holds for the third and fourth friends. By the multiplication principle the number of lists is $3 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 24$. Check with small cases: two friends give $3 \cdot 2 = 6$ lists, namely $12, 13, 21, 23, 31, 32$, which matches the pattern $3 \cdot 2^{n-1}$. The idea: when every step has the same number of options no matter what came before, multiply.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
